events.title: Traditional foundation of Rome
events.summary: Varro's foundation date for Rome, 21 April (the Parilia) 753 BC, fixed by Atticus and Varro in the late Republic; Fabius Pictor gave 748/747, Cincius Alimentus 729/728, Timaeus 814/813 (the same year as Carthage).
events.detail: The date is a learned construct: Varro's friend L. Tarutius of Firmum even cast Rome's horoscope. Archaeology shows Iron Age huts on the Palatine from the 9th-8th centuries, a fortification wall on the north slope of the Palatine (Carandini's excavations, dated c. 730-720 by him, contested), and the first beaten-earth Forum floors around 700-650. The synoecism of village communities into a single city is a process of the 8th-7th centuries, not an act. Romulus, the twins, the asylum and the Sabine women are etiological legend.
scholarship: Forsythe, A Critical History of Early Rome (2005) 78-93
events.debate: Carandini reads the Palatine wall as evidence of a real founding act c. 750; most (Cornell, Forsythe, Smith) prefer gradual state formation.

events.title: Numa Pompilius and the religious calendar
events.summary: Tradition credits the Sabine king Numa (r. 715-673) with the pontiffs, flamines, Vestals, Salii, the twelve-month calendar adding January and February, and the temple of Janus whose closed doors signified peace.
events.detail: The story that Numa was a pupil of Pythagoras was already rejected on chronological grounds by Cicero and Livy (Pythagoras flourished c. 530). In 181 BC 'books of Numa' were allegedly found in a chest on the Janiculum and burned by the praetor Q. Petillius as subversive. The Regia in the Forum, traditionally Numa's house, has building phases from the late 7th century.

events.title: Destruction of Alba Longa under Tullus Hostilius
events.summary: Traditionally under Tullus Hostilius (r. 673-642) Rome fought Alba Longa, the duel of the Horatii and Curiatii decided the war, and the Alban dictator Mettius Fufetius was torn apart by chariots for treachery; Alba was razed and its people moved to the Caelian.
events.detail: The story explains Rome's later presidency of the Latin festival on the Alban Mount (feriae Latinae) and the presence of Alban gentes (Julii, Servilii, Quinctii, Cloelii) among the patricians. No urban site of Alba Longa has been securely identified; scattered Iron Age cemeteries around Lake Albano suggest villages rather than a city.

events.title: Battle of Alalia (Sardinian Sea)
events.summary: Sixty Phocaean penteconters from Alalia in Corsica met a combined fleet of 60 Carthaginian and 60 Etruscan (Caeretan) ships; the Phocaeans won a 'Cadmean victory', lost 40 ships, and abandoned Corsica for Rhegium and then Elea.
events.detail: Herodotus records that the Caeretans stoned their Phocaean prisoners to death, were afflicted with a plague, and consulted Delphi, which ordered annual funeral games; this links Caere to Delphi a generation before Rome. The battle shows the Etrusco-Punic alignment that underlies the Pyrgi tablets and the first Rome-Carthage treaty. Date c. 540-535.

battle.significance: Phocaean victory in name but they abandoned Corsica; Etruscans secured Corsica, Carthage Sardinia. The Greek third side (Phocaeans of Alalia) is not a polity in this dataset.

events.title: Reforms attributed to Servius Tullius
events.summary: Servius Tullius (trad. r. 578-535) is credited with the first census, the five property classes and 193 centuries of the comitia centuriata, the four urban tribes, and a city wall; the census allegedly counted 80,000 men (Fabius Pictor in Livy).
events.detail: The full 193-century system with its bronze-asses ratings is anachronistic for the 6th century (coinage begins c. 300); Cornell and Forsythe accept a simpler early classis/infra classem division tied to hoplite equipment. Claudius' Lyons speech (ILS 212) preserves an Etruscan tradition identifying Servius with Mastarna, companion of Caelius Vibenna, whom the François Tomb paintings at Vulci show freeing Caile Vipinas and killing a 'Cneve Tarchunies Rumach' (Gnaeus Tarquinius of Rome). The so-called Servian wall of cappellaccio tufa may be 6th century in parts, but the surviving circuit is of 378 BC.
scholarship: Forsythe, A Critical History of Early Rome (2005) 108-115

events.title: Draining and paving of the Forum; the Cloaca Maxima
events.summary: Tradition assigns the drainage of the Forum valley by the Cloaca Maxima to the Tarquins; archaeology shows the Forum was landfilled and given its first pebble pavement c. 625-600 BC, the moment Rome becomes recognisably urban.
events.detail: The Cloaca was originally an open channel; the surviving vaulted conduit in peperino and travertine is of the late Republic. The Comitium, Regia and the Volcanal/Lapis Niger area also show 6th-century monumental phases; the Lapis Niger cippus carries one of the oldest Latin inscriptions (mid-6th century) naming a 'recei' (rex).
scholarship: Holloway, The Archaeology of Early Rome and Latium (1994)

events.title: Expulsion of the Tarquins and end of the monarchy
events.summary: After Sextus Tarquinius raped Lucretia, L. Junius Brutus and L. Tarquinius Collatinus led an aristocratic coup that expelled Tarquinius Superbus, then besieging Ardea, and replaced the king with two annual magistrates.
events.detail: The Lucretia story is a moral drama modelled partly on Greek tyrant-expulsions (Brutus' feigned stupidity, the Delphic oracle, the Peisistratid parallel of 510 BC at Athens, which may have influenced the date). The underlying fact, the fall of a monarchy at the end of the 6th century, is broadly accepted: the Regia ceases to be a residence, the rex sacrorum survives as a priestly relic, and the Capitoline temple dedication and first Carthage treaty (Polybius) cluster at the start of the Republic. What replaced the king is debated: two consuls from the start (the Fasti), a single praetor maximus (Livy 7.3.5 on the nail law), or a period of Etruscan condottieri such as Porsenna. Collatinus was soon exiled merely for bearing the name Tarquinius.
scholarship: Forsythe, A Critical History of Early Rome (2005) 147-155
Ogilvie, A Commentary on Livy Books 1-5 (1965) 218-232
events.debate: Alföldi (Early Rome and the Latins, 1965) argued for a later date c. 470 and Etruscan rule continuing; Gjerstad down-dated the kings too. Cornell defends a date c. 509-505 because the Fasti and the Polybian treaty fit it.

events.title: First annual magistrates of the Republic
events.summary: The Fasti list five consuls in 509 (Brutus, Collatinus, Sp. Lucretius Tricipitinus, P. Valerius Publicola, M. Horatius Pulvillus), an overcrowding that betrays later reconstruction of the year.
events.detail: The chief magistrates were probably originally called praetores (Livy 3.55.12; Festus on 'praetor maximus'), with 'consul' a later title. The Fasti for the early 5th century contain names of families later plebeian (Iunii, Cassii, Minucii, Genucii, Sempronii), which Cornell uses to argue the patriciate was not yet closed and that the list is substantially authentic rather than invented. A 'lex vetusta' required the praetor maximus to drive a nail into the wall of the Capitoline temple each Ides of September, so the nails could count years.
events.debate: Whether the dual collegial consulship goes back to 509 or developed later (De Martino, Heurgon) is unresolved.

events.title: Dedication of the Temple of Jupiter Optimus Maximus
events.summary: The great triad temple of Jupiter, Juno and Minerva on the Capitol, begun by the Tarquins, was dedicated on the Ides of September in the first year of the Republic by the consul M. Horatius Pulvillus.
events.detail: Its podium measured c. 53 x 62 m (cappellaccio tufa foundations survive in the Palazzo Caffarelli), making it among the largest temples of the Mediterranean in its day. The terracotta cult statue and the quadriga on the roof were commissioned from Vulca of Veii (Pliny). Pulvillus' rival Valerius' family supposedly tried to disrupt the dedication with false news of his son's death. The dedication date anchored the 'era of the Capitol' and the nail-count of years; Polybius dates the first Carthage treaty to the consuls of the year 28 years before Xerxes' crossing.
scholarship: Hopkins, The Genesis of Roman Architecture (2016)
events.debate: Some (e.g. Hopkins vs. Mura Sommella's critics) question whether the vast podium supported a single 6th-century temple of that size.

events.title: First treaty between Rome and Carthage
events.summary: Polybius transcribed from bronze tablets in the treasury of the aediles a treaty of the first consuls: Romans and allies were not to sail beyond the Fair Promontory except under duress, trade in Libya and Sardinia only before a herald or scribe, and Carthage was not to harm Ardea, Antium, Laurentum, Circeii, Tarracina or any Latin city subject to Rome.
events.detail: The treaty claims Roman suzerainty over coastal Latium, matching the regal Rome of Livy book 1, and treats Rome as a junior trading partner of a Punic maritime power. Polybius says even the most learned Romans could barely read its archaic Latin. The Fair (Kalon) Promontory is probably Cape Farina (Ras Sidi Ali el Mekki) north of Carthage, or Cape Bon. The Pyrgi tablets (c. 500) show comparable Etrusco-Punic ties at Caere.
scholarship: Walbank, A Historical Commentary on Polybius I (1957) 337-345
events.debate: Mommsen and others redated it to 348 because Livy and Diodorus know no treaty before 348; most now accept Polybius' date (Walbank, Cornell), not least because the archaic language and context make better sense c. 509.

events.title: Battle of the Silva Arsia
events.summary: Veii and Tarquinii, supporting the exiled Tarquins, fought the new Republic in the Arsian wood; Brutus and Arruns Tarquinius killed each other in a cavalry duel, and a divine voice (Silvanus) proclaimed that the Etruscans had lost one man more.
events.detail: The Roman matrons mourned Brutus for a year. Publicola celebrated the first triumph of the Republic (the Fasti Triumphales record a triumph over the Veientes and Tarquinienses on 1 March 509). The story belongs to the patriotic legend of the founding year.
events.locName: Silva Arsia, between Rome and Veii (unlocated)

sides.losses: 11,301 (one more than the Romans, per the divine voice)

battle.significance: Legendary first victory of the Republic and death of Brutus.

events.title: Lex Valeria de provocatione (509)
events.summary: Publicola is said to have carried a law granting citizens the right of appeal (provocatio) to the people against a magistrate's capital sentence, and to have lowered the fasces before the assembly.
events.detail: Livy reports three Valerian laws of appeal (509, 449, 300) and himself notes that the 300 law was 'the third, always by the same family'. Most scholars regard the 509 and 449 laws as retrojections of the 300 law (or of the Twelve Tables' rule that only the comitia maximus could pass capital sentence).
scholarship: Oakley, A Commentary on Livy Books VI-X, vol. IV (2005) on 10.9
events.debate: Doublet of the lex Valeria of 300.

events.title: Lars Porsenna's attack on Rome
events.summary: Lars Porsenna of Clusium seized the Janiculum and blockaded Rome; Roman legend tells of Horatius Cocles holding the Sublician bridge, Mucius Scaevola burning his hand in Porsenna's brazier, and the escape of the hostage Cloelia, after which Porsenna made peace in admiration.
events.detail: A different tradition survives: Tacitus says Rome was surrendered to Porsenna (dedita urbe), and Pliny cites a treaty in which Porsenna forbade the Romans to use iron except for agriculture. The likeliest reconstruction (Cornell, Forsythe) is that Porsenna captured Rome, perhaps not to restore Tarquin but in his own interest, and lost his grip after his son's defeat at Aricia. The Roman custom of 'selling the goods of King Porsenna' at auctions (Livy 2.14.1) hints at a real occupation. Porsenna's name may be an Etruscan title (purth, a magistracy).

battle.significance: Roman tradition claims a moral victory; Tacitus and Pliny imply Rome capitulated. Porsenna's peace returned the Septem Pagi to Veii and took hostages.

scholarship: Forsythe, A Critical History of Early Rome (2005) 147-149
events.debate: Whether Porsenna took Rome. Livy's dating to 508/507 depends on the inflated Varronian fasti.

events.title: Battle of Aricia
events.summary: A Latin army reinforced by Aristodemus of Cumae defeated and killed Arruns, son of Porsenna, beneath the walls of Aricia, breaking Clusine power in Latium; Etruscan survivors fled to Rome and settled in the Vicus Tuscus.
events.detail: The battle is attested independently in a Cumaean chronicle used by Dionysius (book 7), which makes it one of the best-founded events of the period and the start of Aristodemus' tyranny at Cumae, where he later sheltered Tarquin. Dionysius places it some 20 years before 492, Livy right after Porsenna's peace; c. 505-504 is usual.

battle.significance: Ends Clusine control of Latium and launches Aristodemus' tyranny at Cumae.

scholarship: Alföldi, Early Rome and the Latins (1965) 56-72
events.debate: The 'Cumaean chronicle' (Alföldi) is hypothetical but widely accepted.

events.title: Migration of Attus Clausus and the Claudii
events.summary: The Sabine noble Attus Clausus of Regillum migrated to Rome with a large following (5,000 clients in Dionysius), was enrolled as a patrician as Appius Claudius, and received land beyond the Anio that became the tribus Claudia.
events.detail: A key piece of evidence for archaic horizontal mobility of elites with private armies of clients, comparable to the Lapis Satricanus 'suodales' of Publius Valerius and the Fabii at the Cremera. Tacitus (Ann. 11.24) has Claudius cite it in his speech on admitting Gauls to the Senate. Suetonius (Tib. 1) dates it to the time of Romulus with Titus Tatius instead.

events.title: Lapis Satricanus inscription
events.summary: A dedication to Mars (Mamars) by 'the companions (suodales) of Poplios Valesios' reused in the foundations of the temple of Mater Matuta at Satricum, found in 1977 and dated c. 500.
events.detail: Poplios Valesios is the archaic form of Publius Valerius, and some identify him with Publicola himself. Whether or not, the stone documents a warlord's sodales operating outside any state structure, the kind of band seen in the Fabian clan war at the Cremera and Attus Clausus' migration, and it shows that names in the early Fasti correspond to real archaic gentes.
events.debate: Identification of Poplios Valesios with Publicola is possible but unprovable.

events.title: Pyrgi tablets: Thefarie Velianas' dedication
events.summary: Three gold tablets (two Etruscan, one Phoenician) found in 1964 at the sanctuary of Pyrgi, Caere's port, record the dedication of a shrine to Uni-Astarte by Thefarie Velianas, ruler (Phoenician 'king over Kysry') of Caere, c. 500.
events.detail: The bilingual is the longest Etruscan-Phoenician text known and shows a Caeretan ruler courting Carthage, the same Tyrrhenian world in which the first Rome-Carthage treaty was concluded. Pyrgi's temples were plundered by Dionysius I of Syracuse in 384.
scholarship: Serra Ridgway, 'Etruscans, Greeks, Carthaginians: the sanctuary at Pyrgi', in Descœudres (ed.), Greek Colonists and Native Populations (1990)

events.title: First dictator: Titus Larcius
events.summary: Facing a threat from the Latins and Sabines, Rome appointed its first dictator, T. Larcius (Livy 2.18 gives 501 or 498 depending on his sources), with Sp. Cassius as master of the horse.
events.detail: Livy admits his sources disagree on who was first dictator and when; some named M'. Valerius. The dictatorship (originally magister populi, with a magister equitum) was a six-month emergency office named by a consul; it may reflect an archaic Latin office (the dictator of Lanuvium, the dictator Latinus who dedicated the Diana grove at Aricia per Cato).

events.title: Dedication of the Temple of Saturn
events.summary: The temple of Saturn at the foot of the Capitol was dedicated on 17 December (the Saturnalia) in 497 according to Livy (others gave 498 or 501); it later housed the aerarium, the state treasury.
events.detail: Its podium is under the eight Ionic columns of the 4th-century AD rebuilding. The temple's early date is one of several dedications clustered in the first decades of the Republic (Saturn 497, Mercury 495, Ceres 493, Castor 484) that suggest a still-prosperous city before the 5th-century recession visible in imports.
scholarship: Ziolkowski, The Temples of Mid-Republican Rome (1992)

events.title: Battle of Lake Regillus
events.summary: The dictator A. Postumius Albus defeated the Latin League, led by Octavius Mamilius of Tusculum with the aged Tarquinius Superbus, near Lake Regillus; Castor and Pollux reportedly fought for Rome and watered their horses at the Juturna spring in the Forum.
events.detail: Postumius vowed a temple to Castor, dedicated in 484; the Ides of Quinctilis became the day of the transvectio equitum, the cavalry parade. Livy places the battle in 499 or 496 (he cites both). Mamilius was killed by T. Herminius. The epic detail (single combats, the divine twins) suggests a heroic poem or family tradition behind the narrative. A dedication to the Dioscuri ('Castorei Podlouqueique qurois') from Lavinium, c. 500, shows the cult was Latin-Greek and already present in the region.
events.locName: Lake Regillus (probably Pantano Secco near Frascati)

battle.significance: Ends Tarquin's hopes of restoration; leads to the Foedus Cassianum of 493 on terms of equality.

scholarship: Ogilvie, A Commentary on Livy Books 1-5 (1965) 285-289
events.debate: Date 499 or 496; location of the lake. The outcome was probably less decisive than claimed since the 493 treaty is between equals.

events.title: Dedication of the Temple of Mercury
events.summary: The temple of Mercury by the Circus Maximus was dedicated on the Ides of May 495; when the consuls quarrelled over who should dedicate it, the people gave the honour to the senior centurion M. Laetorius, who also founded a guild of merchants (collegium mercatorum).
events.detail: The placement outside the pomerium by the Aventine and the river harbour links it to trade with Greek and Etruscan merchants; the episode is also an early instance of popular assertion against the consuls before the secession of 494.

events.title: Death of Tarquinius Superbus at Cumae
events.summary: The last king died in exile at Cumae at the court of the tyrant Aristodemus; Livy notes that news of his death prompted the patricians to begin oppressing the plebs.
events.detail: Aristodemus inherited Tarquin's property and later seized Roman grain ships sent to buy corn during the famine of 492, using it as a claim against Rome.

events.title: Colonists sent to Signia
events.summary: Livy reports that Signia, founded by Tarquinius Superbus, received a fresh draft of colonists in 495 to hold the Monti Lepini against the Volsci.
events.detail: Signia's polygonal walls (late 6th-4th century) and the temple on its acropolis survive. Early 'Latin colonies' like Signia, Norba, Velitrae and Circeii were joint foundations of Rome and the Latin League placed on the Volscian front.

events.title: First Secession of the Plebs and creation of the tribunate
events.summary: Plebeian soldiers crushed by debt bondage (nexum) refused to fight and withdrew to the Mons Sacer (or the Aventine, per Piso); they returned after Menenius Agrippa's fable of the belly and the limbs, having won sacrosanct tribunes of the plebs to protect them.
events.detail: The plebs swore a lex sacrata making anyone who harmed a tribune sacer (killable with impunity). Sources disagree on the first number of tribunes (two, four or five) and their names (L. Sicinius Bellutus and L. Iunius Brutus are suspiciously named). The plebeian aediles, guardians of the temple of Ceres, appear at the same time. The secession created a state within the state with its own assembly (concilium plebis), officers and treasury, and set the template of the Struggle of the Orders. Modern debate concerns whether 'plebs' were the whole non-patrician population or a poorer, organised movement (Raaflaub, Mitchell), and whether the patriciate was already closed.
events.locName: Mons Sacer (by the Anio, 3 Roman miles from Rome)
scholarship: Raaflaub (ed.), Social Struggles in Archaic Rome (1986; 2nd ed. 2005)
Forsythe, A Critical History of Early Rome (2005) 170-177
events.debate: Mons Sacer vs Aventine. Dionysius turns the episode into long Thucydidean speeches. Mitchell (Patricians and Plebeians, 1990) denies the patrician-plebeian division is archaic at all.

events.title: Foedus Cassianum
events.summary: Sp. Cassius concluded a treaty of perpetual peace and mutual defence between Rome and the Latin League: equal shares of booty, alternating command, and no aid to each other's enemies.
events.detail: The bronze text stood behind the Rostra and Cicero says it was still remembered in his day. Dionysius preserves its terms: 'Let there be peace between the Romans and all the cities of the Latins as long as heaven and earth remain in the same place'. Legal rights of conubium, commercium and the ius migrationis shared by Latins probably date from this framework. The joint foundation of 'Latin colonies' on the Volscian front (Signia, Velitrae, Norba, Antium, Ardea, Circeii, Satricum, Setia, Sutrium, Nepet) followed the treaty's logic.
scholarship: Alföldi, Early Rome and the Latins (1965) 111-122
events.debate: Whether booty was split equally between Rome and the League collectively (thus Rome as half) or among all members; whether command alternated (Festus' 'praetor' at the Ferentine spring).

events.title: Dedication of the Temple of Ceres, Liber and Libera
events.summary: Sp. Cassius dedicated the temple of Ceres, Liber and Libera on the Aventine, vowed by A. Postumius during a famine in 496; it became the religious centre of the plebs, seat of the plebeian aediles and archive of plebiscites and senatus consulta.
events.detail: Pliny says the Greek artists Damophilus and Gorgasus decorated it with painting and terracotta and signed their work in Greek verse, the earliest attested Greek artists at Rome. The triad mirrors the Eleusinian Demeter, Iacchus and Kore, probably via Cumae, and the temple's Greek priestesses were recruited from Naples and Velia (Cicero).
events.locName: Aventine slope above the Circus Maximus
scholarship: Ziolkowski, The Temples of Mid-Republican Rome (1992)

events.title: Capture of Corioli
events.summary: During the consul Postumus Cominius' attack on the Volscian town of Corioli, the young patrician Gnaeus Marcius forced his way through the gate and took the town, earning the cognomen Coriolanus.
events.detail: Livy remarks that the consul's name had been eclipsed so thoroughly that only the treaty with the Latins preserved it. Corioli was already forgotten by Pliny's day (he lists it among vanished peoples of Latium). The cognomen derived from a place is anachronistic for 493.

sides.strength: town garrison and relief army from Antium

events.title: Famine and grain embassies of 492
events.summary: After the secession left fields unsown, Rome sent grain buyers to Etruria, Cumae (where Aristodemus seized their ships) and Sicily, where 'the tyrant' supplied corn; in 491 Coriolanus allegedly proposed withholding it unless the tribunate was abolished.
events.detail: Dionysius names Gelon of Syracuse as the Sicilian donor, an anachronism (Gelon took Syracuse in 485) already noticed by Dionysius himself, who criticised Licinius Macer and Gellius for it; Livy merely says 'the tyrant'. The annalistic record of famines (492, 456, 440-439, 411) and grain purchases from Etruria, Campania and Sicily probably derives from the pontifical tables and is among the more credible 5th-century data.
scholarship: Garnsey, Famine and Food Supply in the Graeco-Roman World (1988) 167-181
Ogilvie, A Commentary on Livy Books 1-5 (1965) 320-322

events.title: Colony at Norba
events.summary: A colony was sent to Norba, on the edge of the Monti Lepini overlooking the Pontine plain, as a citadel against the Volsci.
events.detail: Norba's superb polygonal walls and gates (2.5 km circuit) survive; the town was destroyed by Sulla's forces in 82 BC and never reoccupied, so the street grid is visible from the air.

events.title: Coriolanus leads the Volsci against Rome
events.summary: Exiled after a tribunician prosecution, Coriolanus joined the Volscian leader Attius Tullius of Antium and led a Volscian army that took a string of Latin towns and camped at the Fossae Cluiliae, five miles from Rome, until his mother Veturia and wife Volumnia persuaded him to withdraw.
events.detail: The temple of Fortuna Muliebris at the fourth milestone of the Via Latina was said to commemorate the women. The story has a real background: the Volscian advance into Latium in the early 5th century, which took Satricum, Antium, Velitrae, Circeii and the Pontine plain from Latin control. But the hero is probably fictitious, or a much reworked folk figure; the list of towns he captured mirrors later Volscian conquests.
events.locName: Fossae Cluiliae, 5 miles from Rome on the Via Latina
scholarship: Cornell, 'Coriolanus: myth, history and performance', in Braund & Gill (eds.), Myth, History and Culture in Republican Rome (2003)
events.debate: Historicity of Coriolanus; Fabius Pictor had him live to old age in exile.

events.title: Treaty with the Hernici
events.summary: Sp. Cassius in his third consulship brought the Hernici of the Sacco valley into the Roman-Latin alliance on the same terms as the Latins, taking two-thirds of their land according to Livy.
events.detail: The Hernici held the strategic wedge between Volsci and Aequi; the triple alliance enabled the slow 5th-century counter-offensive. Livy's land confiscation is probably a confusion; Dionysius describes an equal treaty.

events.title: Agrarian proposal and execution of Spurius Cassius
events.summary: Sp. Cassius, three times consul, proposed distributing public land to plebs and Latins in 486; next year he was condemned for aiming at kingship (adfectatio regni) and executed, by the quaestors or by his own father, and his house razed.
events.detail: The tale of the first agrarian law looks heavily coloured by the Gracchan crisis; but the motif of the aristocrat who courts the plebs and is killed for 'regnum' (Cassius 485, Maelius 439, Manlius 384) seems to be a real archaic pattern of elite self-policing. A bronze statue of Ceres made from his confiscated property bore the inscription 'ex Cassia familia datum'.
scholarship: Forsythe, A Critical History of Early Rome (2005) 192-193
events.debate: Gracchan retrojection of the agrarian law is likely.

events.title: Dedication of the Temple of Castor
events.summary: The son of the dictator Postumius dedicated the temple of Castor (and Pollux) in the Forum beside the spring of Juturna, fulfilling his father's vow at Lake Regillus.
events.detail: Excavations (Danish-Italian, 1980s) found the 5th-century podium under the Augustan-Tiberian rebuilding whose three standing columns are a Forum landmark. The temple was a meeting place of the Senate and later a weights-and-measures office.
scholarship: Nielsen & Poulsen (eds.), The Temple of Castor and Pollux I (1992)

events.title: Battle of Himera
events.summary: Gelon of Syracuse and Theron of Acragas annihilated a large Carthaginian expedition under Hamilcar the Magonid at Himera; Greek tradition placed it on the same day as Salamis (Herodotus) or Thermopylae (Diodorus).
events.detail: Carthage paid 2,000 talents indemnity, and Gelon's Demareteion coinage and the Himera victory temple (the 'Temple of Victory', Doric) commemorate it. Carthage withdrew from Sicilian expansion for seventy years, turning to its African hinterland. The battle frames the western Greek world into which Rome's first contacts (grain from Sicily, Cumae) fall.

sides.losses: army destroyed; Hamilcar killed or self-immolated

battle.significance: Halts Carthaginian expansion in Sicily for 70 years; Syracusan hegemony under the Deinomenids.

events.title: Disaster of the Fabii at the Cremera
events.summary: The gens Fabia undertook the war against Veii as a private enterprise, garrisoning a fort on the Cremera with 306 Fabii and their clients; they were ambushed and all killed, leaving a single boy to continue the line.
events.detail: Ovid dates the disaster to the Ides of February; Livy (6.1.11) and Tacitus treat 18 July as the day of both the Cremera and the Allia. The '306' and the surviving child are legend (and modelled on the 300 Spartans), but the clan war of a gens with its clients against a neighbour fits the archaic world of the Lapis Satricanus. The Fabii vanish from the Fasti for a decade after 479, which may reflect a real catastrophe. The Porta Carmentalis through which they marched was thereafter ill-omened (the 'Porta Scelerata').
events.locName: River Cremera (Fosso della Valchetta) near Veii

battle.significance: Veii seizes the Janiculum briefly; war ends with a 40-year truce in 474.

scholarship: Richardson, 'The Fabii and the Cremera', in Richardson & Santangelo (eds.), Andreas Alföldi in the Twenty-First Century (2015)
events.debate: Date (13 Feb vs 18 July) and the role of the gens as a private army.

events.title: Naval battle of Cumae
events.summary: Hiero I of Syracuse, answering an appeal from Cumae, destroyed an Etruscan fleet off Cumae, ending Etruscan naval dominance in the Tyrrhenian and isolating the Etruscan cities of Campania.
events.detail: Hiero dedicated captured Etruscan helmets at Olympia; two survive, one in the British Museum inscribed 'Hiaron son of Deinomenes and the Syracusans to Zeus, Tyrrhenian spoils from Cumae'. Pindar's first Pythian celebrates the victory. Syracuse then planted a short-lived base on Pithecusae (Ischia). Weakened by the defeat, Etruscan Capua fell to the Samnites in 423.

battle.significance: End of Etruscan sea power in the southern Tyrrhenian.

scholarship: Meiggs & Lewis, Greek Historical Inscriptions no. 29 (helmet)

events.title: Forty-year truce with Veii
events.summary: The first Veientine war ended with a 40-year truce (indutiae), a typical early Roman instrument; Veii paid grain and money.
events.detail: Truces of fixed length (Veii 474, 40 years; Tarquinii 351, 40 years; Caere 353, 100 years; Volsinii 308, 30 years) were archaic Italian practice that pre-dated the formal foedus.

events.title: Lex Publilia Voleronis
events.summary: The tribune Volero Publilius, a former centurion who had resisted being enrolled as a common soldier, carried a law that tribunes be elected by an assembly organised by tribes rather than curiae.
events.detail: The consul Appius Claudius' resistance led to a battle in the Forum; his army then deserted against the Volsci and he decimated it, the first recorded decimation. The tribal assembly of the plebs (concilium plebis tributum) based on residence weakened patrician clientage in the curiate system. Number of tribunes may have been raised to four or five at this time.
